places.name: Thải Chi Cốc
places.look: A shallow forest valley opens off the road, its floor striped with herb beds that step down toward the river below. At the valley mouth sit four moss-grey stone hermits in a row, each cradling a lingzhi in its lap and facing the road as if judging who may enter. The air smells of bitter roots and the smoke of drying sheds.
places.lore: Thải Chi Cốc is a minor sect (tiểu tông môn) of herb growers and alchemists (luyện đan sư) sworn to Tùng Đào Cung. Its founders were lingzhi pickers who had left the world, and the valley still sings their old song of the four hermits at every planting. Since Nghiêm Linh Chi became valley-mistress in 1000, the river's orphans have worked the fields and learned their letters in the drying sheds, and many never leave.
places.history: In 480 lingzhi pickers who had turned their backs on the world settled this valley under the pines of Cửu Khúc Xuyên and founded Thải Chi Cốc, singing the song of the four hermits as they cleared the ground. Tùng Đào Cung, lord of the basin since the Age of First Gates, took the little sect under its banner. In 520 the valley planted the first spirit-herb (linh dược) fields along the river, and for a century travellers said the valley smelled of medicine before they saw a roof. The four stone hermits at the valley mouth are thought to date from those years, though no one agrees whose hands carved them. The valley kept out of its lord's wars, sending pills (đan dược) downriver rather than disciples to the field. In 1000 Nghiêm Linh Chi became valley-mistress and opened the herb fields to the orphans of the river, and the valley has been louder ever since. The riverside town of Hà Bạn Trấn answers to it today.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a narrow forested valley seen from above at an angle. Herb beds in bands of green, ochre and dusky purple step down the valley floor toward a strip of river at the lower edge; low grey-tile drying sheds sit among them, and terraces climb at the valley head to a slim three-roof pagoda hall with moss-green tiles, the tallest outline. At the valley mouth, four tiny seated stone hermit statues in a row, the signature element. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, soft shadows across the terraces, thin wisps of drying-shed smoke. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the valley footprint.
levels: More drying sheds and a stone furnace house with a tall chimney; the herb terraces climb further up both valley walls.
A second pagoda hall joined to the first by a covered stair, an upper grove of shaded lingzhi logs, and long orphan dormitories along the lower fields.

places.name: Lãng Đào Môn
places.look: On low wooded ground just back from the river stands a sect gate made of two great river-boat hulls, upturned and set on end so their keels meet overhead in a pointed arch. Behind it, tarred timber halls and rope sheds climb a gentle rise, and a path of crushed shell runs down toward the landing at Đào Sa Thị. The whole place smells of pitch and wet hemp.
places.lore: The ferrymen of the Nine-Bend River banded together as Lãng Đào Môn in 790, a minor sect (tiểu tông môn) under Tùng Đào Cung that carries most of the river trade. Its disciples learn water arts (thủy pháp) on a deck before they learn them in a hall, and a ferryman who retires burns his first oar at the gate of hulls. Since the Ferry War the sect counts its lost boats aloud each spring, one by one.
places.history: Before 790 the boatmen of Cửu Khúc Xuyên worked alone, each family with its own landing and its own feud. In 790, the year the War of Broken Halberds broke out on the border plain of three sects, they banded together as Lãng Đào Môn under Tùng Đào Cung, to carry the river trade as one. From 800 gold-washers gathered on the sands beside them, and the market of Đào Sa Thị gave the sect its landing. For nearly four centuries its ferries tied the river towns together while Tùng Đào took the tolls. In 1172 the quarrel with Lạc Hà Tông over the river tolls on the Ngư Ca border turned to war, and Lãng Đào's ferries burned; in 1173 Lạc Hà raiders fired its boats at the Đào Sa landing. The Ferry War ended two years after that raid with the tolls split and no land changed, and neither side forgives. Giang Cửu Khúc heads the sect today, and its slipways have not been quiet since.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature on low forest ground near a river. At its front, the signature gate: two upturned boat hulls standing on end, dark-tarred, keels meeting in a pointed arch. Behind it a short climb of dark timber halls under grey-tile roofs, stacked oars and coiled rope, topped by a three-roof watch pagoda, the tallest outline. A pale shell path runs toward the footprint edge, where a sliver of riverbank and one slipway show. Warm golden-hour light from the top left glinting on the tar. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A covered slipway and a second hall for rope-makers; the watch pagoda gains a lantern storey to signal ferries at night.
A stone dock of its own on the river bend with rows of rebuilt ferries drawn up, and a four-roof pagoda rising behind the gate of hulls.

places.name: Đào Thanh Thành
places.look: A walled river city under endless pine, its quays set high up the bank on tall stone steps. Below them, at low water, a row of old drowned quay pillars stands in the current like a broken fence, marking where the city once met the river. When the wind turns, the forest above roars like surf, and the streets go quiet to listen.
places.lore: Tùng Đào Cung founded the city in 300 on the river below its forests, and named it for the sound of the pine waves heard from the seat above. Timber merchants, river traders and the families of Tùng Đào's outer disciples live here. On windy evenings the townsfolk climb the walls to hear the pines, and a child who sleeps through the first great wind of autumn is teased for a year.
places.history: Tùng Đào Cung took the river basin of Cửu Khúc Xuyên in the Age of First Gates, and in 300 founded Đào Thanh Thành on the river below its forests. The city grew as the palace's market and river gate, shipping timber and pine resin downstream. In 700 a great flood on the Nine-Bend River drowned three villages, and Tùng Đào moved the city's quays up the bank; the old pillars were left standing in the water. The city prospered through the long peace of the North Star Compact, and is said to have sent boats and grain north in the Long Lake War of the Age of Vein Wars. When the Ferry War burned Lãng Đào's ferries, its merchants felt it in their ledgers, and the split tolls still sour the wharf taverns. Today it is the busiest city on the river, and the pines above it are as loud as ever.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a rectangular walled river city among dark pines: tight rows of grey-tile roofs, green-glazed eaves on the city hall, and a three-storey gate tower as the tallest outline. Along the river edge, tall stone stair-quays climb the bank, and just offshore a line of broken old quay pillars stands in blue water, the signature element. Pine forest presses against the walls on the landward side. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, pale glints on the river. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the city and its strip of bank.
levels: A second row of wharf warehouses along the high quays and a pine-roofed listening terrace on the upper wall.
An outer wall reaching to the forest edge, a covered bridge over the river, and a five-roof bell pagoda that answers the pine waves.

places.name: Đào Sa Thị
places.look: Where the river spreads its sand into the sea, a market sprawls across the flats on stilts. Rows of wooden washing cradles stand in the shallows, rocked by washers in wide straw hats, and at low tide the whole flat glitters with fine gold. Along the landing lie the charred ribs of burned ferries, left where they sank.
places.lore: Around 800 gold-washers learned that after a thousand washings the river sand gives up its gold, and Đào Sa Thị grew beside Lãng Đào Môn. It is a market of scales, sieves and quick hands under Tùng Đào's peace, where anyone who keeps their head down can find work at a cradle. The washers still tell how Triệu Huyết Y hid among them for two years after the hunt that killed her master, and lately some swear they have seen her again.
places.history: Before 800 the sand flats at the river mouth held little but gulls and driftwood. Around 800 gold-washers learned that after a thousand washings the river sand gives up its gold, and Đào Sa Thị grew beside the new ferry sect Lãng Đào Môn, which made its landing here. For three centuries the market lived on gold dust and ferry traffic under Tùng Đào Cung's peace. In 1090 Thiên Xu, Tùng Đào and Băng Tâm killed the demonic-path (ma đạo) master Mặc Huyết Sinh, and his last disciple Triệu Huyết Y escaped; in 1092 she hid for two years among the gold-washers here. A generation ago the Ferry War broke out, and in 1173 Lạc Hà raiders burned Lãng Đào's boats at the Đào Sa landing. For years afterward the washers fished nails from the river along with their gold. The burned ribs still lie at the landing, and the market washes on.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a sprawling stilt market on golden sand flats at a river mouth: low grey-tile and thatch roofs on posts, no wall, and one tall tarred signal mast as the tallest outline. Across the shallows, rows of small wooden washing cradles on stilts, the signature element, with gold specks glinting in the water around them. A blackened line of burned ferry ribs lies beside a timber landing at one side. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the flats.
levels: A raised boardwalk links the stalls to a rebuilt landing, with a red-doored assay house at its head.
A market square on piles behind a timber palisade, a small customs pagoda flying Tùng Đào's colours, and washing cradles out to the far sandbars.

places.name: Hà Bạn Trấn
places.look: A low riverside town whose fishing lanes all end at the water. At its upstream corner a great timber waterwheel turns beside a mill house, grinding roots from Thải Chi Cốc into powder, and its creak carries to the road. Herb sacks stand stacked on the short jetties, waiting for boats.
places.lore: Hà Bạn Trấn was a fishing hamlet until 290, when the river's new course ran past its door and it grew into a town on the new bank. It now answers to Thải Chi Cốc, grinding and shipping the valley's herbs downriver. The townsfolk have a saying for every stroke of luck: the river came to us, so we do not chase it.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a low town of grey-tile roofs inside a modest rectangular wall, open on the river side where short jetties reach into the water. At the upstream corner, a large dark timber waterwheel beside a mill house, the signature element and the tallest outline. Small boats along the bank and stacked herb sacks by the mill. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the town and its bank.
levels: A second waterwheel and a stone mill house, with a covered herb wharf along the bank.
The wall runs along the river with a water gate, and a row of mills turns in a cut channel beside the town.

places.name: Lâm Hạ Trấn
places.look: The town sits so deep in the shade of old beeches that its roofs are green with moss even in summer. Between the houses stand round timber granaries raised on squat stone staddles shaped like mushrooms, so that no rat can climb them. At noon the lanes are cool and dim, and smell of grain dust.
places.lore: In 600 Tùng Đào Cung set its northern granaries in the shade of Lâm Hạ Trấn, so the grain would keep, and the town has lived as a storehouse ever since. Its people are granary-keepers, coopers and rat-catchers, proud that their grain does not spoil. Felling a shade tree inside the town is the one crime the elders never pardon.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a low cluster of moss-green grey-tile roofs inside a small rectangular wall, almost hidden under the broad crowns of old beeches. Among the houses, several round timber granaries with conical roofs raised on mushroom-shaped stone staddles, the signature element. A river edge at one side with a grain jetty. Warm golden-hour light from the top left breaking through the canopy in patches. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the town.
levels: More round granaries on staddle stones and a timber fence around the storehouse quarter.
A stone granary hall with a tall vented roof under the oldest beeches, and a full town wall with a grain gate on the river.

places.name: Tuyết Ốc Thôn
places.look: In winter the village almost vanishes: low turf-roofed houses sunk half into the ground, chimneys smoking through the drifts. Each house is marked by a tall red-painted door-pole so neighbours can find each other under the snow. In summer the poles stand oddly tall over a cluster of grassy mounds by the upper river.
places.lore: Winters on the upper river are so deep that the houses of Tuyết Ốc have been built half under the snow since at least 340. Families dig tunnels from door to door and visit underground all winter. A new bride paints her husband's door-pole fresh red on her first spring in the village.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a tight cluster of low, half-sunken houses with turf and grass roofs beside a narrow upper river, with patches of snow around them. Over each house rises a tall thin red door-pole, the signature element, a little forest of red lines taller than the roofs. Smoke from short chimneys. Warm golden-hour light from the top left on the snow. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village.
levels: A longhouse dug into the riverbank for winter gatherings, with snow-tunnels from every door.
A small timber stockade and a raised storehouse above the snowline, and door-poles crowned with carved finials.

places.name: Hàn Mai Thôn
places.look: A handful of grey-tile houses sits around a small snowy square, and in the middle of the square grows one gnarled winter plum behind a low bamboo fence. In the cold months its red blossoms are the only colour for days of travel. Villagers bow to it on their way down to the river.
places.lore: In 420 a winter plum bloomed through the snow above a buried child, and the diggers found her alive; the village was named Hàn Mai. The tree in the square is said to have grown from a cutting of that plum. Every child born in winter is carried to the tree before it is given a name.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a handful of low grey-tile houses around a little square on a snowy riverbank. In the centre of the square, one gnarled dark plum tree with bright red blossoms inside a low bamboo fence, the signature element. A narrow path down to the river. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, red petals glowing against white snow. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village.
levels: A small shrine roof beside the plum and a few new houses facing the square.
A walled courtyard around the plum with a gate arch, and a second, younger plum planted at the village edge.

places.name: Bạch Lang Thôn
places.look: The village circles a hollow at its heart, ringed with white-limed boulders: the old den of the white wolf king. Children run between the houses with wolf-tooth charms clicking at their necks. A path from the hollow leads down to the river, where women beat laundry on flat stones.
places.lore: Thôi Khinh Hồng of Tùng Đào Cung slew the white wolf king of Cửu Khúc Xuyên, and in 456 the village built on its den was named Bạch Lang. Its children wear wolf-tooth charms. Each spring the boulders around the den are limed white again, and the village says that the year they are left grey, the wolves will come back.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a ring of low grey-tile and thatch houses around a central grassy hollow, the hollow rimmed by a circle of chalk-white boulders, the signature element. A footpath runs from the hollow to a strip of river with flat washing stones. Forest edge on one side. Warm golden-hour light from the top left making the white stones glow. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village.
levels: A timber fence around the village and a small shrine at the lip of the den.
A stone wall with a gate carved with a wolf's head, and a hunters' lodge beside the den.

places.name: Đông Lưu Thành
places.look: A long stone quay wall runs through an empty meadow, its rusted iron mooring rings hanging over grass where boats once tied up. Behind it stand the roofless stubs of warehouses, and a fresh scar of sand shows where a spring flood has opened up an old paved street. The living river runs past at a distance, along the edge of the bed.
places.lore: Mortal boatmen built Đông Lưu Thành on a great bend of the northern river in 90, long before any sect held this land. They gave the river spirit a pig every spring for safe passage, until the spirit stopped answering; ten years later the river left them, and the city was abandoned in 281. Old boatmen still say all things flow east, and do not finish the saying.
places.history: In 90, in the Wild Age when only hermits and beasts held the land, mortal boatmen built Đông Lưu Thành on a great bend of the northern river. From 100 they gave the river spirit a pig every spring for safe passage, and the city lived well on its boats. Late in the Age of First Gates, Tùng Đào Cung took the river basin, and the city fell under its protection. In 270 the river spirit stopped answering the boatmen's offerings. Ten years later the river left them, cutting a new course across the plain, and in 281 Đông Lưu Thành was abandoned; all things flow east. Some say the spirit itself stayed behind in a pool somewhere on the old course. For more than nine centuries the city lay under silt and grass, until a spring flood in 1198 uncovered its old street on the dry bed, and children found coins of a city no one remembers.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of broken verticals beside a dry, grassy river bed: a long stone quay wall standing in open meadow, hung with a row of rust-red iron mooring rings over the grass, the signature element; behind it the jagged, roofless wall stubs of old warehouses; a short strip of uncovered grey paving in pale flood sand. No intact roofs, only a few fallen grey tiles in the grass. A thin glint of living river along one edge of the footprint. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, long shadows from the wall stubs. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Hổ Khiếu Cương
places.look: A long bare ridge rises between the river's bends, its crest banded with dark and pale rock like a tiger's flank. The wind funnels through a notch in the crest with a low growl, and now and then a real roar answers it from the boulders below. No path crosses it.
places.lore: Herders of the lower basin say a roar on this ridge carries across all nine bends of the river, and they do not graze its slopes. A great tiger keeps its lair among the boulders, and hunters who go up for its pelt seldom come down the way they went. Tùng Đào's riders go around the ridge, not over it.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a long bare highland ridge with no roofline: the crest banded in alternating dark grey and pale ochre rock like tiger stripes, the signature element, with a narrow wind notch near its middle. Tumbled boulders and dark scrub on the flanks, and one shadowed cave hollow among the boulders. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, deep shadow on the far slope. No buildings, no text, no animals larger than specks, nothing outside the ridge.

places.name: Cửu Cao Phái
places.look: Out of a reed marsh rise slender red-lacquered crane-roost towers, each topped with a broad platform of woven reed where the great birds stand and preen. Behind them, terraced halls climb a low wooded rise to a four-roof pagoda. The cry of cranes overhead never quite stops.
places.lore: Crane riders who tamed the first cranes of the nine marshes founded Cửu Cao Phái in 700, a minor sect (tiểu tông môn) of beast tamers (ngự thú sư) sworn to Thiên Xu Tông. Its riders carried the Pivot's messages over Phá Quân's fort in the rebellion, and now circle Tinh Tủy Mạch day and night. In 1197 its head Ung Hạc Minh tamed a crane king that will let no one else ride it, and the young riders compete for the honour of grooming it.
places.history: In 700 crane riders tamed the first cranes of the nine marshes in Dao Quang Lĩnh and founded Cửu Cao Phái; the old line runs that the crane cries in the nine marshes and is heard in the sky. That same year the cranes were first seen landing at Hạc Quy Thôn on the same day every year, and the school has ridden the first of them since. When Phá Quân Môn rose against Thiên Xu, the crane riders stayed loyal, and in 872 they carried the Pivot's messages over the rebel fort. At the war's end in 874 Thiên Xu gave Cửu Cao Phái the rebels' holdings. In 1010 Ung Hạc Minh was born in Hạc Quy Thôn, the year the cranes stayed a month longer, and Ung Hạc Minh now heads the school. After Băng Tâm's claim to Tinh Tủy Mạch was rejected by the Pivot, the school's cranes were set to circle the vein day and night. In 1197 Ung Hạc Minh tamed a crane king that will let no one else ride it.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a minor sect seat on a low wooded rise above a green reed marsh. Terraces of pale stone climb the rise to a four-roof pagoda with grey-tile roofs and red-lacquered pillars, the tallest outline. In front, in the marsh, several slender red-lacquered crane-roost towers topped with round reed platforms, the signature element, with a few white crane specks on them. Warm golden-hour light from the top left on the reeds and water. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: More roost towers out across the marsh and a long crane stable hall on the lower terrace.
A tall roost tower for the crane king beside a five-roof pagoda, and a stone landing terrace where riders come down from the sky.

places.name: Khai Dương Thành
places.look: A walled port city where the northern road meets a river mouth and the sea. Its east gate tower carries a great polished bronze disc that catches the first light before dawn, so the gate seems to burn while the streets below are still dark. Masts crowd the river quays under the walls.
places.lore: Thiên Xu Tông founded Khai Dương Thành on the northern road in 280, naming it for a star of the Northern Dipper. In 900 its gate was rebuilt to face the morning star, and travellers say the city wakes before the sun: bakers, porters and ferrymen are at work in the dark. Late sleepers are called guests here, even if they were born in the city.
places.history: A generation after Thiên Xu Tông extended its protection over Dao Quang Lĩnh, in 280, it founded Khai Dương Thành on the northern road where it reaches the sea. The city became the Pivot's northern port, shipping ore and timber by river and by sea. Through the Age of the North Star Compact it grew quietly rich, far from the wars of the south. When Thiên Xu founded Thanh Bách Thành on the same road in the first years of the Compact, Khai Dương became the road's harbour end. In the Phá Quân rebellion of the Age of Vein Wars, the city fed and shipped the Pivot's forces in the mountains above. In 900 its gate was rebuilt to face the morning star and the bronze disc was set over it; travellers say the city wakes before the sun.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a rectangular walled port city at a river mouth on the sea: grey-tile roofs in neat rows, river quays crowded with small masts, and a sea mole at one corner. On the east side, a tall gate tower crowned by a large polished bronze disc, the signature element and the tallest outline, flaring gold in the light. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, bright reflections on the water. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the city and its quays.
levels: A stone sea mole with warehouses along it, and a second bronze disc on the river gate.
An outer harbour wall, a lighthouse tower on the mole, and a new walled quarter climbing the riverbank inland.

places.name: Bích Khê Trấn
places.look: A small walled town on a brook so green it looks dyed. Below the walls the stream runs over shallow stone weirs where jade-pickers kneel, sorting pebbles into baskets by colour. Polishing wheels hum in the workshops along the main street.
places.lore: A jade-green brook below the ridges gave Bích Khê Trấn its name around 300, and its trade in river jade. Pickers comb the brook bed after every flood, and the carvers in town turn the pebbles into seals and hairpins for Thiên Xu's officials. When a match is made, the bride's family gives an uncut pebble from the brook as its promise.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a low town of grey-tile roofs inside a small rectangular wall beside a brook of vivid jade-green water stepped by shallow stone weirs, the signature element. Baskets and tiny workshops along the bank; forest and ridges at the far edge. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, the green water glowing. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the town and its brook.
levels: A carvers' street with a covered market, and a stone footbridge across the green brook.
A larger wall, a jade hall with a green-glazed roof, and weirs stepping the brook far upstream.

places.name: Thanh Bách Thành
places.look: A walled city of grey roofs and dark, narrow cypresses on the northern road, a cypress standing over every courtyard. Outside its north wall lies a small round crater pond, glassy black at the rim, where a star fell in 980. Ore carts and officials' carriages pass through its gates all day.
places.lore: Thiên Xu Tông founded Thanh Bách Thành on its northern road in 520, and the city is named for its green cypresses. In 980 a star fell near the city; the fragment was sold to Thối Tinh Môn for three years of the city's taxes, and the crater filled with rain. Townsfolk toss a coin into the pond for luck, though the clerks say the city has paid that star enough already.
places.history: Thiên Xu Tông founded Thanh Bách Thành on its northern road in 520, in the first years of the North Star Compact, to guard the road between the heart and Khai Dương Thành. Cypress seedlings were planted in every courtyard, and the city took their name. It grew as a waystation for ore carts, officials and the Pivot's patrols in Dao Quang Lĩnh. In the Phá Quân rebellion of the Age of Vein Wars its gates stayed shut to the rebels, and it quartered Thiên Xu's troops. In 980 a star fell near the city; the fragment was sold to Thối Tinh Môn for three years of the city's taxes. The crater pond outside the north wall is all the city kept of it, and the old cypresses still stand over the courtyards.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a rectangular walled city with grey-tile roofs and many tall, narrow dark-green cypresses rising between them, a gate tower as the tallest roofline. Just outside the north wall, a small round crater pond with a glassy black rim, the signature element. A road runs through the gates. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, the cypresses casting long thin shadows. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the city and its pond.
levels: A second market quarter inside the walls and a shrine pavilion on the crater pond's rim.
An outer wall enclosing the crater pond, and a tall tax hall with stacked roofs among the oldest cypresses.

places.name: Ba Quang Thôn
places.look: A fishing village on the shore of a chain of small mountain lakes stepping down a grassy slope, its boats drawn up on the gravel. At midday the lakes throw so much light that the village seems to stand in a blaze. Flat reed rafts lie on the beach, ready for the evening nets.
places.lore: Light glints so brightly on the mountain lakes at Ba Quang that travellers have taken the village for a fire since at least 600, and more than one has run up with a bucket. Its people net lake fish and ferry Cửu Cao Phái's riders across the water. The elders squint their whole lives, and a squint is thought handsome here.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a few low grey-tile and reed-roofed houses on the gravel shore of a chain of small bright lakes stepping down a grassy slope, the signature element, each lake a mirror of gold light. Reed rafts and small boats on the beach. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, strong sparkles on the water. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village and its lakes.
levels: A timber boat landing and a drying rack for nets along the lowest lake.
A small walled hamlet with a lakeside shrine and a crane perch for Cửu Cao's riders.

places.name: Hạc Quy Thôn
places.look: A quiet marsh-edge village of reed-thatched and grey-tile houses on a slow river. In the meadow beyond, the villagers keep a crescent-shaped landing pool dug in the turf and edged with flat grey stepping stones, where the cranes come down each year. They clear its weed by hand all summer.
places.lore: Cranes return to the marshes here on the same day every year, and since 700 the village where they land has been called Hạc Quy; Cửu Cao Phái rides the first of them. Ung Hạc Minh was born here in 1010, the year the cranes stayed a month longer. On landing day the whole village stands silent around the crescent pool until the last bird folds its wings.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a handful of reed-thatched and grey-tile houses on a slow river at a marsh edge. Beside them, in a green meadow, a crescent-shaped pool edged with flat grey stepping stones, the signature element. Reeds and still marsh water around. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no people or birds larger than specks, nothing outside the village and its meadow.
levels: A reed-roofed watching shelter beside the crescent pool and a few new houses along the river.
A timber fence, a small shrine to the cranes, and a rest hall for Cửu Cao's riders.

places.name: Lộc Uyển Thôn
places.look: A hillside village of log houses above a high meadow where deer gather each spring. At the meadow's edge stands a black stone stele carrying Thiên Xu's ban on hunting, and shed antlers are heaped around its foot. A rail fence keeps the village goats off the deer's grass.
places.lore: Deer have gathered each spring in the high meadow of Lộc Uyển since before 380, when Thiên Xu forbade hunting there. Children collect the antlers the stags shed and lay them at the stele as a gift to the Pivot. Poachers from outside are rare; the villagers report them before the deer have even scattered.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a few log houses with grey-tile roofs on a forested slope above a high green meadow. At the meadow edge, a black stone stele with a heap of pale shed antlers around its foot, the signature element, its face blank in the art. A rail fence and a stream below. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no people or deer larger than specks, nothing outside the village and meadow.
levels: A gamekeeper's lodge beside the stele and a fenced herb garden.
A small walled hamlet with a gate house of the Pivot's wardens and a covered antler hall.

places.name: Phụ Tinh Phong
places.look: A glacier peak stands beside taller neighbours, white ice over dark rock. Its broad shoulder holds a flat terrace cut into the ice, still bristling with rows of rusted iron stakes where weapon racks once stood. At night a single faint star hangs just above its summit.
places.lore: From 760 the disciples of Phá Quân Môn drilled here at night under the faint companion star beside the Dipper, as if to prove the small star could break armies too. Since the rebellion was crushed no one drills here; the stakes remain and the wind sings over them. Thiên Xu's patrols come up now and then only to look, and go down again.
places.history: Thiên Xu's protection reached Dao Quang Lĩnh in the Age of First Gates, and this glacier peak, too cold to farm or mine, was left to the wind. Late in the Age of the North Star Compact, Phá Quân Môn was founded in the mountains below it as a vassal of the Pivot. In 760, the year Chung Hoài Cực died, Phá Quân's disciples began to drill at night on Phụ Tinh Phong under the faint companion star, cutting a terrace into the shoulder and setting iron racks for their weapons. Whether the drills were meant for the Pivot's enemies or the Pivot itself, no one asked until a century later, when Hạ Lang Tinh led Phá Quân Môn against its lord. Within a few years Thiên Xu destroyed Phá Quân Môn, and the night drills ended. The racks rotted down to their iron stakes, which still stand in rows on the terrace. No sect holds the peak today.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a sharp glacier peak with no roofline: white ice and blue shadow over dark rock, a flat terrace cut into its broad shoulder holding rows of tiny rust-red iron stakes, the signature element. A faint pale star-glint just above the summit. Golden-hour light from the top left warming the snow, cold blue on the far side. No buildings, no text, no figures, nothing outside the peak.

places.name: Trích Tinh Phong
places.look: The roof of the heartland: a dark rock peak rising clear of the clouds, its summit ending in a thin stone needle. Strips of white cloth tied around the needle stream in the wind, and below it a pilgrims' road of a thousand rock-cut steps runs up the spine of the ridge. On clear nights the stars seem to rest on the needle's tip.
places.lore: Thiên Xu's first watchmen climbed Trích Tinh Phong in 260 and reported that one could pluck the stars by hand, and the peak has carried that name since. By 1100 the pilgrims' road up it had been cut into the rock in a thousand steps. Pilgrims tie a white strip at the needle and make a wish on a star; it is bad luck to say which one.
places.history: In 260, in the Age of First Gates, Thiên Xu's first watchmen climbed Trích Tinh Phong and came down saying one could pluck the stars by hand. The Pivot, founded under the stars of the Northern Dipper, kept the summit as a place to watch them. Two centuries later its patrols found the Star Marrow vein, Tinh Tủy Mạch, high near the peak, and posted a guard that has never been withdrawn. Through the Age of the North Star Compact pilgrims climbed to the needle by goat paths and tied their white cloths at the top. By 1100 the pilgrims' road had been cut into the rock in a thousand steps. Since Băng Tâm's claim to the vein was rejected by the Pivot, pilgrims climb under the eyes of a doubled guard and circling cranes.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a tall dark rock peak with no roofline, rising above a collar of cloud, its summit a thin stone needle wrapped with fluttering white cloth strips, the signature element. Snow in the gullies, and a faint thread of path along the ridge spine below. Warm golden-hour light from the top left on the needle, deep shadow on the far side. No buildings, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the peak.

places.name: Tinh Tủy Mạch
places.look: High on a black rock face near Trích Tinh Phong, seams of silver-white star marrow thread through the stone and glitter like frost even at noon. A low stone breastwork and a guards' fire pit sit on a ledge in front of the face. Cranes wheel over it in slow rings.
places.lore: Thiên Xu found the Star Marrow vein (linh mạch) high near Trích Tinh Phong in 470 and posted a guard that has never been withdrawn. Its qi (linh khí) runs to Metal and Earth, heavy and cold as iron. In 1188 Băng Tâm Các claimed it before the Pivot and was refused; since then the guard has been doubled, and Cửu Cao's cranes circle it day and night.
places.history: At the end of the Wild Age stones fell from the sky on Thiên Tuyền Nguyên, and the star iron in them drew the first cultivators to the heart; some say the marrow in this mountain is kin to that iron, though no one has proved it. In 470 Thiên Xu found the Star Marrow vein high near Trích Tinh Phong and posted a guard that has never been withdrawn. Through the long Compact the vein lay quiet near the border of Băng Tâm Các, never fought over. In 1188 Băng Tâm claimed Tinh Tủy Mạch before the Pivot; the claim was rejected, and Sở Ngọc Hồ withdrew in silence. In 1189 Thiên Xu doubled the guard, and Cửu Cao Phái's cranes began to circle the vein day and night. The silence from the desert seat has not yet been broken.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a black high-mountain rock face with no roofline, seamed with bright silver-white glittering veins, the signature element. On a ledge before it, a low curved stone breastwork with a tiny glowing fire pit. Snowfields above, tiny white crane specks circling. Warm golden-hour light from the top left making the veins flash. No roofs, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the rock face and ledge.

places.name: Phá Quân Môn
places.look: On a high mountain shoulder, a gate arch split clean down the middle still stands, each half leaning away from the other, with seven iron star-studs running across its broken lintel. Behind it, scorched walls and the stump of a watchtower climb the slope. Grass grows in the old parade ground, and little else.
places.lore: Hạ Lang Tinh founded Phá Quân Môn in 720 as a vassal of Thiên Xu, naming it for the Army-Breaker, the Dipper's seventh star. In 870 Hạ Lang Tinh led it against its lord to win by war the land the Compact forbids, and in 874 Thiên Xu destroyed it; Đỗ Tinh Hà took Hạ Lang Tinh's spear. Miners of Dao Quang Lĩnh say the seventh stud on the gate glows on the night of the fall.
places.history: In 720 Hạ Lang Tinh founded Phá Quân Môn in the mountains of Dao Quang Lĩnh as a vassal of Thiên Xu, named for the Dipper's seventh star, the Army-Breaker. It held the high passes for the Pivot and trained hard; within two generations its disciples were drilling at night on nearby Phụ Tinh Phong. In 870 Hạ Lang Tinh led Phá Quân Môn against its lord, to win by war the land the North Star Compact forbids. Thiên Xu laid siege to the fort, and in 872 Cửu Cao's crane riders carried the Pivot's messages over it. In 874 Thiên Xu destroyed Phá Quân Môn; Đỗ Tinh Hà took Hạ Lang Tinh's spear, and Cửu Cao Phái received the rebels' holdings. The fort was never rebuilt, and Thiên Xu keeps the ruin as a warning to its vassals.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of broken verticals on a high mountain shoulder: a stone gate arch split down the middle, its two halves leaning apart, a row of seven small iron studs on the broken lintel, the signature element. Behind it, fire-blackened wall stubs and the jagged stump of a watchtower climbing the slope, a grassy parade ground in front. No intact roofs. Snow and grey rock around. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, long shadows through the split. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Bằng Sào Nhai
places.look: A sheer cliff of pale rock towers over the forest, and on a ledge near its top sits a nest the size of a farmhouse, woven from whole pine trunks bleached grey. Feathers longer than a man lie in the scree below. Nothing else nests within sight of it.
places.lore: A roc nests on these cliffs and hunts over the steppe and forest below. Herders drive their flocks under the trees when its shadow crosses, and Cửu Cao's riders fly their cranes wide of the cliff. Its fallen feathers are prized by fletchers and talisman (phù lục) makers.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a sheer pale cliff with no roofline, a huge nest of bleached grey pine trunks on a ledge near its top, the signature element. Scree and dark forest at its base, a few long feathers in the scree. Warm golden-hour light from the top left on the cliff face. No buildings, no text, no creatures larger than specks, nothing outside the cliff.

places.name: Môn Am
places.look: A small hermitage of white-plastered halls climbs a steep slope beside the ice fields, inside an orchard of old pear trees whose branches are white with rime most of the year. From below, the rimed orchard looks like a hillside in full blossom even in deep winter. A single three-roof bell pagoda stands above the trees.
places.lore: Môn Am, the Gate Hermitage, is the old seat of Lê Hoa Am, a hermitage (am) of women ice cultivators and a minor sect (tiểu tông môn) sworn to Băng Tâm Các. The grey sisters hold the gate here, where outsiders meet the hermitage, under the prioress Mạnh Tĩnh Chi, while the white nuns went up to the glacier of Lăng Tuyệt Phong in 702. A nun founded it in 600 after a snow fell like pear blossom overnight in the eighth month, and when Chúc Long Sơn rumbled in 1199 the nuns prayed all winter.
places.history: In 600 a snow that fell like pear blossom overnight in the eighth month brought a nun to the ice fields of Ngọc Hồ Sơn, and she founded Lê Hoa Am where it had fallen. The hermitage swore itself to Băng Tâm Các, which had held the empty ice for more than a century. Its nuns planted pear trees around their halls, and the rime on the branches gave the place the look of its name. The Tiêu family's village of Hòe Âm below came to answer to the hermitage. In 1020 Thái Lê Tuyết became abbess. In 1150 the Tiêu clan sent its first son to the gate; he was turned away for being a son, and became a hunter. In 1199 Chúc Long Sơn rumbled under the ice for the first time since the eruption that buried Hồ Thiên Phái, and the nuns prayed all winter.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a minor sect seat on a steep snowy slope: small white-plastered halls with grey-tile roofs on narrow terraces, climbing to a three-roof bell pagoda, the tallest outline. All around the halls, an orchard of gnarled pear trees with branches thick with white rime like blossom, the signature element. Blue-white ice fields at the upper edge. Warm golden-hour light from the top left turning the rime pink-gold. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A meditation hall cut into the ice field edge and a wider ring of rimed pear trees.
A second bell pagoda higher on the slope, a covered stair between the two, and a walled guest court below for pilgrims.

places.name: Hòe Âm Trấn
places.look: A small harbour town where a river reaches the sea, and from its back gate an avenue of ancient locust trees climbs toward the mountains, their crowns meeting overhead in a green tunnel. Fishing boats and the hermitage's supply carts share one narrow quay. In early summer the locust blossom drops on the road like pale snow.
places.lore: Locust trees planted by the Tiêu family shaded the road into the mountains, and around 520 their village took the name Hòe Âm; it now answers to Lê Hoa Am. In 930 a hunter of the town found a sealed cave on the mountain with a sword's cold light behind the seal; he ran, and never found it again. Every hunter since has looked for that cave, and tavern talk names more dead swordsmen behind its seal than the mountain could hold.
places.history: In the first years of the North Star Compact the Tiêu family planted locust trees along the road from the river mouth into the mountains, to shade the carts that climbed to the ice. Around 520 the cluster of houses at the foot of their avenue took the name Hòe Âm, for the locusts' shade. The village fished, hunted the lower slopes and carried supplies up the mountain road, and grew into a small harbour town. After the hermitage of Lê Hoa Am was founded on the heights, the town came to answer to it and to carry its stores. In 930 a hunter of Hòe Âm found a sealed cave on the mountain with a sword's cold light behind the seal; he ran, and never found it again. Since then every hunter of the town has looked for that cave, and none has found it. Half a century ago the Tiêu clan sent a son to the hermitage's gate and saw him turned away, and he too took up the hunter's bow. The locusts still shade the road, older now than any house beneath them.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a low harbour town of grey-tile roofs inside a rectangular wall at a river mouth on the sea, a narrow quay with small fishing boats. From its landward gate, a double row of broad old locust trees runs uphill with their crowns meeting, the signature element. Mountains begin at the far edge. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the town and its avenue.
levels: A stone quay with a hunters' market, and the locust avenue extended further up the mountain road.
A larger wall with a harbour gate, a Tiêu family hall with a two-tier roof, and a waystation for Lê Hoa Am's pilgrims at the avenue's end.

places.name: Đỗ Quyên Thôn
places.look: A fishing village sits on a grey shore under steep slopes that turn blood-red with azaleas each spring. Its low houses are roofed with dark stone slabs against the wind, and its boats lie hauled up on black volcanic shingle. In bloom the slope looks like a fire about to come down on the roofs.
places.lore: Azaleas bloom red on the slopes above Đỗ Quyên Thôn each spring, and since at least 640 the villagers have said they are the dead of the eruption. No one picks them. On the first day of bloom the village leaves rice cakes at the foot of the slope and does not fish.
places.history: Fishers lived on this shore below the ice mountains while Hồ Thiên Phái still stood on the ice nearby, trading fish for the school's furs and salt. When Chúc Long Sơn erupted in the Age of Seven Seats and buried the school, ash fell on the village and the sea ran warm and grey for a season. The survivors stayed, and their dead were buried on the slope above the houses. Băng Tâm Các claimed the empty ice two generations later, and the village came under its rule. In time red azaleas covered the slope where the graves lay. By 640 the villagers said that the azaleas blooming red above Đỗ Quyên Thôn each spring were the eruption's dead, and the custom of leaving rice cakes at the foot of the slope had begun. No one in the village picks them, and when the mountain rumbled again in the last winter the azaleas were the first thing the fishers looked at in spring.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a few low houses with dark stone-slab roofs on a grey shore, small boats on black shingle. Above them, a steep slope blanketed in bright red azalea blooms, the signature element. Grey sea at the near edge. Warm golden-hour light from the top left deepening the red. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village and its slope.
levels: A small timber jetty and a shrine at the foot of the azalea slope.
A low stone sea wall, a boat shed, and a terraced path up through the azaleas to a lookout.

places.name: Hoàng Oanh Thôn
places.look: In a sheltered coastal valley, a ring of grey-tile houses stands among bare willows hung with woven straw bird shelters. All winter the shelters flash yellow with orioles, and their song carries down to the boats. Snow lies on the ridges all around.
places.lore: Orioles winter in the valley of Hoàng Oanh Thôn, the only birdsong in the ice mountains, and the village has woven shelters for them since at least 850. Nuns from the hermitage up the mountain are said to come down in winter only to listen. A child who throws a stone at an oriole must sleep one night with the goats.
places.history: The valley was a fishing cove long before it had a name, sheltered from the north wind by the ridges around it. Late in the Age of Seven Seats it came under Băng Tâm Các with the rest of the ice mountains. At some time no one recorded, orioles began to winter among its willows, the only birdsong anywhere in the ice mountains. By 850 the birds were known across Băng Tâm's land, and the village had taken the name Hoàng Oanh for them. The villagers began weaving straw shelters for the birds and hanging them in the willows each autumn. Nuns from Lê Hoa Am are said to walk down the mountain in winter only to hear them. The orioles have never failed to come, and the village takes their arrival as the true start of its year.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a ring of low grey-tile houses in a small coastal valley, with bare willow trees hung with round woven straw bird shelters, the signature element, dotted with tiny yellow specks. Boats at a short shingle beach, snowy ridges at the edge. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village.
levels: A timber boat landing and more willows planted along the stream.
A small walled hamlet with a listening pavilion among the willows and a stone jetty.

places.name: Hồi Lộ Phong
places.look: A steep ice peak is wrapped in a switchback stair carved into its flank, the steps doubling back so often that the stair looks like white thread wound around a spindle. Wind-scoured snow fills the turns. From below, climbers on it seem to vanish and reappear at random.
places.lore: Hồ Thiên's disciples carved a stair of ice up Hồi Lộ Phong around 300; it bends so often that companions lose each other in plain sight. The school is long gone, but the cold has kept the stair. Băng Tâm's disciples climb it roped together, and quote the old line: the mountain turns, the road bends, and you are gone.
places.history: Hồ Thiên Phái was founded on the ice below Chúc Long Sơn in 210, and this peak above its ice fields became the school's training ground. Around 300 its disciples carved a stair of ice up Hồi Lộ Phong, bending so often that companions lost each other in plain sight. When Chúc Long Sơn erupted in 425 and buried the school, the stair stood high above the ash and lava. When Băng Tâm Các claimed the empty ice of Ngọc Hồ Sơn in the Age of Seven Seats, it found the stair still whole. Its disciples have climbed it roped together ever since, and have still lost one now and then. No sect holds the peak itself.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a steep ice peak with no roofline, its flank wound with a tight switchback stair of pale carved ice steps, the signature element, like a white thread around a spindle. Wind-blown snow in the turns, dark rock showing at the ridges. Warm golden-hour light from the top left catching the steps, cold blue shadows. No buildings, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the peak.

places.name: Lê Hoa Am
places.look: The highest summit on the continent, a white glacier pyramid standing clear above a sea of cloud, with a cairn of pale stones on its very top. On a shelf of rock and ice on its flank a small hermitage of white-plastered halls hangs a bronze bell, ringed by frost-white stones.
places.lore: Lăng Tuyệt Phong is the Upper Hermitage of Lê Hoa Am, a hermitage (am) of women ice cultivators, a minor sect (tiểu tông môn) sworn to Băng Tâm Các. In 702 the founder Kỷ Hoa Ảnh raised it on the glacier, hung the bell cast from frozen lightning at the heart of the Pear-Frost Ring and planted ice pears round it; the white nuns live here under the abbess Thái Lê Tuyết, and the grey sisters hold the gate below. Băng Tâm's climbers reached the summit in 480 and left the cairn, and Băng Tâm's disciples still climb it before a long seclusion.
places.history: No climb of the continent's highest peak is remembered from the Wild Age or the Age of First Gates; even Hồ Thiên's disciples, who carved the stair on Hồi Lộ Phong, left no record of its top. Tần Ngưng Sương founded Băng Tâm Các in the Age of Seven Seats, and within a generation the sect had claimed the empty ice of Ngọc Hồ Sơn. In 480 the sect's climbers reached the summit of Lăng Tuyệt Phong and saw all the mountains small. They left a cairn of pale stones at the top. In the centuries since, Băng Tâm's disciples have climbed it as a rite before long seclusion, and the sect has never set a building on it. No one claims the peak; the cold holds it.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a tall white glacier pyramid with no roofline rising out of a sea of soft cloud, clearly the tallest form on the map, a tiny cairn of pale stones on its point, the signature element. Blue crevasses on its flanks. Warm golden-hour light from the top left gilding the summit, the cloud sea below in pink and gold. No buildings, no text, no figures, nothing outside the peak.

places.name: Chúc Long Sơn
places.look: A black cone rises out of the ice fields, its flanks streaked with old lava under a skin of snow. In its crater a dull red glow shows through a lid of ice, like the half-open eye of something asleep. Steam drifts from cracks around the rim and freezes into feathers of rime.
places.lore: Ice hunters have said since the Age of First Gates that the Torch Dragon sleeps under Chúc Long Sơn and lights the mountain when it dreams. In 425 the mountain erupted under the ice and buried Hồ Thiên Phái with its founder Khúc Hồ Già. In 1199 it rumbled for the first time since that eruption, and the nuns of Lê Hoa Am prayed all winter.
places.history: In 120 ice hunters already told that the Torch Dragon slept under Chúc Long Sơn and lit the mountain when it dreamed. In 210 Khúc Hồ Già founded Hồ Thiên Phái on the ice below the fire mountain, where snow flies in the eighth month. In 425 Chúc Long Sơn erupted under the ice and buried the school with its founder, and Ngọc Hồ Sơn lay empty for forty-five years. Băng Tâm Các claimed the ice after those empty years and built nothing near the cone. For centuries the mountain slept, and only the red glow in its crater showed it was alive. In 1199 it rumbled under the ice for the first time since the eruption, and the nuns of Lê Hoa Am prayed all winter.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a black volcanic cone with no roofline rising from white ice fields, its flanks streaked with dark lava under thin snow. In the crater, a lid of ice with a dull red glow beneath it, the signature element, like a sleeping eye. Thin steam wisps at the rim, frosted white. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, the red glow answering it from below. No buildings, no text, no figures, nothing outside the mountain.

places.name: Băng Phách Mạch
places.look: Below the ice mountains, a round cave mouth opens in a cliff, rimmed with ice so white it glows faintly blue, like the moon seen through mist. Inside, pillars of ice give off a cold light of their own. Frost feathers grow on the rocks for a long way around the entrance.
places.lore: Băng phách, the ice soul, is an old name for the moon, and Băng Tâm opened this spirit vein (linh mạch) below the ice mountains in 760. Its qi (linh khí) feeds the sect's ice cultivators and is fierce enough to freeze a careless breath in the throat. The storm peaks loom close, and beasts drawn to the vein's cold make the approach perilous.
places.history: Hồ Thiên Phái held these mountains from 210, but the deep cold under them was never tapped before the eruption of 425 emptied the land. Băng Tâm Các claimed the empty ice of Ngọc Hồ Sơn in the Age of Seven Seats, and for nearly three centuries searched the ice mountains for a vein worthy of its arts. In 760, the year it also founded Hồi Lan Thành on the desert coast, the sect opened the Ice Soul vein, Băng Phách Mạch, below the ice mountains, and named it for the moon. Since then the vein has fed the sect's ice cultivators far from the desert seat. Its approach, close under the storm peaks, remains one of the most feared roads in Băng Tâm's lands.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a dark cliff below snowy ice mountains with no roofline, a round cave mouth rimmed in glowing moon-white and pale blue ice, the signature element, faint ice pillars glimmering inside. Frost-covered rocks around the entrance. Warm golden-hour light from the top left on the snow, the cave giving off its own cold blue glow. No buildings, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the cliff.

places.name: Băng Tâm Các
places.look: Băng Tâm Các's white halls climb a black lava mountain on a sheet of blue glacier ice, raised on the ruin of Hồ Thiên Phái, with a great Vessel Hall on the summit and a tall white pagoda behind it. At the mountain's foot the green-tiled tip of one old pagoda roof still stands out of a bare field of black lava, and a ring of jade-green light glows up through the ice.
places.lore: Băng Tâm Các, the Pavilion of the Ice Heart, is a great sect (đại tông môn) of sword cultivators (kiếm tu); its name comes from the old line that the ice heart sits in the jade vessel. In 470, when the sect claimed the empty ice of Ngọc Hồ Sơn, Tần Ngưng Sương moved it onto the ruin of Hồ Thiên Phái and laid the Jade Vessel Array into the ice over the buried vent; the steam stopped and the birds came back. Sở Ngọc Hồ has led the sect since 1010 as keeper of the Jade Vessel, with Tiết Hàn Mai as first elder. Hồ Thiên Phái, buried by Chúc Long Sơn in 425 with its founder Khúc Hồ Già, lies beneath the halls, and the sect leaves the ruin as it lay.
places.history: In 210 Khúc Hồ Già founded Hồ Thiên Phái on the ice of Ngọc Hồ Sơn, below the fire mountain Chúc Long Sơn, where snow flies in the eighth month. In 230 Khúc Hồ Già forged the sword Phi Tuyết from ice that never melts. In the school's best years its disciples carved the winding ice stair of Hồi Lộ Phong. In 425 Chúc Long Sơn erupted under the ice and buried the school with its founder, and Ngọc Hồ Sơn lay empty. A year later steam still rose from the ice where Hồ Thiên had stood, and no bird sang there. Two generations later Băng Tâm Các claimed the empty ice and left the ruin as it lay. The villagers of Đỗ Quyên Thôn still say the red azaleas on their slopes are the eruption's dead.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of broken verticals on a flat tundra shore: a field of black frozen lava with frost in its cracks, and rising from it only the green-tiled, curled-eave tip of one buried pagoda roof, the signature element, with a few broken roof ridges nearby. Grey water at one edge. No intact buildings. Warm golden-hour light from the top left on the green tiles. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.

places.name: Hàn Giao Chử
places.look: Out on a frozen tundra lake, a lone low islet of black rock is ringed by a coiling pressure ridge of ice that wraps around it like a serpent's body. In the thaw the ridge cracks and groans. Bones of deer and wolves lie bleached on the rock.
places.lore: Far north of Ngọc Hồ Sơn a cold flood-dragon (giao) coils around this islet, and hunters say its body is the ice ridge itself. Those who cross the frozen lake give the islet a wide berth. In hard winters its breath rises in a white column that can be seen from the shore.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a small black-rock islet with no roofline in a frozen grey-white lake, encircled by a thick coiling ridge of blue-white pressure ice shaped like a serpent's body, the signature element. A few pale bones on the rock. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, blue shadows in the ice folds. No buildings, no text, no creatures larger than specks, nothing outside the islet and its ring of ice.

places.name: Hàn Diễm Khẩu
places.look: High on the ice mountains, a crack in the glacier breathes out pale blue flames that dance over the snow without melting it. The ice around the vent is glassy and scorched dark at the lip. Downwind, sulphur stains the snow yellow.
places.lore: Fire runs under the ice of Băng Tâm's land, and here it escapes as cold blue flame. Alchemists (luyện đan sư) prize its heat for furnaces that must not crack in the frost, but the ice around it is treacherous. Since Chúc Long Sơn rumbled, the nuns of Lê Hoa Am have watched this vent as closely as the mountain.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a long crack in a high glacier with no roofline, pale blue flames rising from it, the signature element, the ice glassy and darkened along its lip. A yellow sulphur stain on the snow to one side. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, the blue flames glowing against it. No buildings, no text, no figures, nothing outside the vent.

places.name: Cựu Các
places.look: Out of red badlands at the desert's edge rises a tall white pavilion of stacked celadon-glazed roofs, pale stone terraces climbing to it. Even at midsummer frost rims its eaves, and a thin cold mist spills from the round well-house at its foot, where the water keeps ice all year. Far beyond, the snow ranges of Ngọc Hồ Sơn stand white against the sky.
places.lore: Cựu Các, the Desert Pavilion, is the old seat of Băng Tâm Các, a great sect (đại tông môn) of sword cultivators (kiếm tu), and is now its outer hall for the desert and the caravan road. Ôn Sa Ngọc keeps the Pavilion's trade here and its desert recruits, the oasis children. The founder's cold well still keeps ice all year, disciples here drink only its water, and a newcomer who flinches at the cup is told to stay until they no longer do. Tần Ngưng Sương founded the sect on this ridge in 440 and moved it to the ice of Ngọc Hồ Sơn in 470.
places.history: In 440 Tần Ngưng Sương founded Băng Tâm Các in the cold north-east, a pavilion for the ice heart, on the high badlands between the desert and the ice fields. In 445 Tần Ngưng Sương made the well water of the desert seat cold enough to keep ice all summer. The sect claimed the empty ice of Ngọc Hồ Sơn and founded Trường Vân Thành in 470, and took the frost coast from Hàn Giang Môn in the war of 492 to 498. In the Desert Road War of 722 to 728 it lost Cô Thành to Phượng Minh's fire, and in the Long Lake War of 940 to 944 won only the right to fish the northern shore of Hạo Nguyệt Hồ. Tần Ngưng Sương died in 1010, and Sở Ngọc Hồ became head and keeper of the Jade Vessel; in 1090 she joined the hunt that killed Mặc Huyết Sinh, and in 1121 Hạng Dạ Bôi knelt to her. In 1188 her claim to Tinh Tủy Mạch was rejected before the Pivot, and she returned without a word and shut herself in the seat's ice hall for a year.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a great sect seat on red-brown badland ridges: pale stone terraces climbing to a tall white pavilion tower of many stacked celadon-green glazed roofs, the tallest outline in its land, its eaves edged with white frost. At its foot a round white well-house with cold mist spilling over its rim; frost-rimmed eaves and the mist together form the signature element. Eroded red gullies and a desert road at the base. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, the frost catching it. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A second ice hall carved into the badland ridge behind the pavilion, and terraces of sword-practice grounds below it.
Twin frost-rimmed side towers flanking the main pavilion, joined by covered bridges, and a ring of cold wells mist-veiling the lower terraces.

places.name: Dạ Quang Môn
places.look: A squat fort of rammed red earth sits on the open steppe, ringed by horse lines and sabre racks. Over its gate, on a pillar, stands a great stone cup carved from a pale stone that glows faint green after dusk. Around it the steppe is trampled bare by hooves.
places.lore: Hạng Dạ Bôi gathered the desert raiders and founded Dạ Quang Môn in 970, a minor sect of the demonic path (ma đạo) known for its blood sabres. Since Hạng Dạ Bôi knelt to Sở Ngọc Hồ in 1121, its riders have guarded the very caravans they used to rob. Lately the young blades drink from the night-glowing cups again, the old raiders' rite before a ride, and Băng Tâm's elders pretend not to see.
places.history: Hạng Dạ Bôi was born in 870 to a caravan guard's family in Trường Vân Thành. In 970 Hạng Dạ Bôi gathered the desert raiders and founded Dạ Quang Môn on the steppe beside the caravan road, bound to no lord. For a century and a half its blood sabres preyed on the caravans of Băng Tâm's desert, and the raiders' camp hardened into a fort. In 1119 Băng Tâm Các marched on it. In 1121 Hạng Dạ Bôi knelt to Sở Ngọc Hồ, and Dạ Quang Môn became a vassal of Băng Tâm, and does not forget; its raiders were made to guard the caravans they used to rob. The lotus village of Liên Đường Thôn, on the caravan road, answers to it. In 1194 its young blades drank from the night-glowing cups again, and Băng Tâm's elders pretended not to see.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a minor sect seat on flat golden steppe: a square fort of red rammed earth with a three-roof timber gate tower, the tallest outline, and over the gate a tall pillar topped by a large pale stone cup glowing faint green, the signature element. Horse lines and racks of curved sabres around the walls, bare trampled earth. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
levels: A second ring of earth walls with stables, and a feasting hall with a dark tiled roof.
A tall watch pagoda over the caravan road and a row of glowing stone cups on the outer wall.

places.name: Trường Vân Thành
places.look: A walled harbour city at the edge of the desert, where a river reaches the sea under the snow mountains. A long roofed caravan gallery runs straight through the city from the land gate to the docks, so goods pass from camel to ship without seeing the sun. On cloudy days a faint shimmer of a ward formation hangs over the walls, and long clouds lie on the peaks behind.
places.lore: Băng Tâm Các founded Trường Vân Thành in 470 at the edge of the desert, under the long clouds over the snow mountains, and it is still the sect's door to the sea. Caravan guards, ship chandlers and Băng Tâm's officers crowd the taverns of the gallery. Hạng Dạ Bôi was born here to a caravan guard's family in 870, and the guard families of the city have never let anyone forget it.
places.history: In 470, the year it claimed the ice of Ngọc Hồ Sơn, Băng Tâm Các founded Trường Vân Thành at the edge of the desert, under the long clouds over the snow mountains. The city became the sea gate of the desert road, and the sect raised a ward formation (trận pháp) over its walls. When Băng Tâm built Cô Thành on the caravan road half a century later, Trường Vân became its supply port. Through the Desert Road War the city sent water and swords to the lone fortress, until Cô Thành fell. In 870 Hạng Dạ Bôi was born here to a caravan guard's family; a century later Hạng Dạ Bôi founded Dạ Quang Môn and raided the caravans that fed the city. Since Dạ Quang Môn knelt to Băng Tâm, its raiders have guarded those caravans instead, and the gallery is busy again.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a rectangular walled harbour city of grey-tile roofs at a river mouth on the sea, with desert sand on its landward side. Straight through its middle runs a long continuous roofed caravan gallery from the land gate to the docks, the signature element. A gate tower of three roofs is the tallest outline; a faint translucent shimmer of a ward dome over the walls. Ships at the quays. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the city.
levels: A second caravan gallery branching to a new dock, and a stone caravanserai inside the land gate.
An outer wall around the docks, a lighthouse on the river mouth, and a taller ward formation pagoda at the city's centre.

places.name: Hồi Lan Thành
places.look: A harbour city on the desert coast, built behind a long curved breakwater that hooks out into the sea and turns the waves back on themselves. Sand-coloured walls enclose low warehouses under pale grey roofs. Ships from the south crowd the still water inside the hook.
places.lore: Băng Tâm Các founded Hồi Lan Thành on the desert coast in 760, after the Desert Road War, so that trade with the south need not trust the desert alone. Its harbour filled with southern ships by 770, once the caravan road was safe. In 1160 a merchant of the city brought the first southern rice through the desert since the war, and Băng Tâm taxed it at half; the rice merchants still toast him at every new year.
places.history: The Desert Road War ended a generation before the city's founding with the border where it had been, and Băng Tâm Các looked for a road south that Phượng Minh's fire could not cut. In 760 it founded Hồi Lan Thành on the desert coast and raised the breakwater that turns the waves and gives the city its name. By 770 the harbour was full of ships from the south, now that the caravan road was safe. The city grew on salt, wool and southern goods, and on the trade that had once passed Cô Thành. In 1160 a merchant of Hồi Lan Thành brought the first southern rice through the desert since the Desert Road War, and Băng Tâm taxed it at half. The sea road and the rice road have both run through the city since.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a rectangular city of sand-coloured walls and pale grey-tile roofs on a desert coast, a gate tower as the tallest roofline. From its harbour a long curved stone breakwater hooks out into blue sea, the signature element, with white surf curling back along its outer face and small ships in the calm water inside. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the city and its breakwater.
levels: A rice market quarter and warehouses along the inner breakwater.
A second hooked breakwater forming a full harbour ring, with a watch pagoda at its tip and a walled merchant quarter outside the old wall.

places.name: Ngư Đàm Thôn
places.look: Behind a bitter salt shore where nothing swims, a small oasis holds a grid of square fish ponds edged with mud brick and shaded by date palms. Low flat-roofed houses of the same brick line the dikes between the ponds. Children with wooden clappers chase the herons off the shallows.
places.lore: Since around 500, fish ponds dug in the oasis have given Ngư Đàm Thôn its name and Băng Tâm's desert its only fish; the sea beside it is too salt and barren to net. Carp travel from here to the seat in water jars. A fish dish at a Băng Tâm feast means it came from Ngư Đàm, and the village is proud of it.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a small oasis on a pale salt shore: a neat grid of square fish ponds with mud-brick edges, the signature element, a few date palms, and low flat-roofed mud-brick houses on the dikes between the ponds. A tiny landing for salt boats at the shore. Warm golden-hour light from the top left on the still pond water. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the oasis.
levels: More ponds dug toward the dunes and a covered jar store by the landing.
A mud-brick wall around the oasis, a water tower, and a small shrine on the central dike.

places.name: Liên Đường Thôn
places.look: In the middle of the open steppe, a hollow of spring-fed ponds blooms pink and white with lotus all summer. A few mud-brick houses with reed roofs stand on the banks, and a wooden viewing pier reaches out over the leaves. Caravans halt on the rise above just to look.
places.lore: Lotus ponds have bloomed at Liên Đường since around 560, and caravans stop just to look. The village now answers to Dạ Quang Môn, whose riders water their horses here and leave the flowers alone. Lotus root and seed are its living, and a lotus seed is pressed into the hand of every traveller who asks the way.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a green hollow in golden steppe filled with ponds of pink and white lotus, the signature element, a few mud-brick houses with reed roofs on the banks and a small wooden pier reaching over the leaves. A caravan track on the rise. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the hollow.
levels: A caravan rest yard on the rise and a second viewing pier.
A low earth wall around the ponds, a lotus pavilion on an island in the largest pond, and a horse trough fed by the spring.

places.name: Mã Minh Thôn
places.look: Round corrals of piled dry stone ring a cluster of felt tents and mud houses on the steppe behind the range. The neigh of horses carries far over the grass. To the west a low hump of sand covers the old wells where the village once stood.
places.lore: Nomad herders drove their horses across the steppe behind the range as early as 100, and their camping ground became Mã Minh Thôn. In 1050 a sandstorm buried its wells, and the village moved a short way east, horses and all. Its herders sell remounts to Băng Tâm's caravans and to anyone else who can pay.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a few felt tents and flat-roofed mud houses on golden steppe, surrounded by several round dry-stone horse corrals, the signature element, with tiny horse specks inside. To one side, a low sand mound over old buried wells. Mountains at the far edge. Warm golden-hour light from the top left. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the village.
levels: New stone-lined wells and a long horse barn with a thatched roof.
A walled horse market, a herders' hall, and corrals spread out across the plain.

places.name: Viên Đề Hạp
places.look: A narrow gorge cuts through the high mountains, its walls hung with vines and its river loud below. A timber plank road pinned to the cliff face runs the length of one wall, and gibbons swing above it, crying on both banks without end. Mist fills the gorge floor at dawn.
places.lore: The gibbons of Viên Đề Hạp cry on both banks without end, and since at least 600 caravan drivers have stopped their ears with wax to cross. Old drivers say the cries are worst for the homesick. No sect holds the gorge, and the plank road is mended by whoever needs it.
places.history: The river cut this gorge through the high mountains of Cô Yên Mạc long before any record was kept. Mortal caravaneers pinned the first planks to its walls to shorten the road between the desert and the lands beyond, though no one remembers when. By 600 caravans used it often, and the gibbons crying on both banks without end had taught the drivers to stop their ears with wax. In the Desert Road War, more than a century later, the plank road is said to have served as a back way for messengers, and both sides burned stretches of it. The planks were renewed after the Pivot's truce. No sect has ever claimed the gorge, and the gibbons have outlasted every war.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of a narrow gorge with no roofline between steep grey mountain walls draped in green vines, a white-water river at the bottom. Along one wall, a thin timber plank road on pegs pinned to the cliff face, the signature element. A few dark gibbon specks in the vines, mist at the gorge floor. Warm golden-hour light from the top left lighting the upper walls, the depths in cool shadow. No buildings, no text, no figures larger than specks, nothing outside the gorge.

places.name: Cô Thành
places.look: On a white salt pan that was once a desert lake stands a square fortress, its walls glazed black and cracked by fire. One corner tower still rises to its full height; the rest have slumped. Salt crust creeps up the foot of the walls like frost.
places.lore: Băng Tâm Các raised Cô Thành in 520, a lone fortress on a desert lake to guard the caravan road; an old poem says the lone fortress looks far toward the jade gate. In the Desert Road War its garrison held out for two years against Phượng Minh's fire, drinking the lake down to salt, before it fell in 726. Caravans pass it in silence, and some leave a cup of water at the gate.
places.history: In 520 Băng Tâm Các raised Cô Thành, a lone fortress on a desert lake, to guard the caravan road between the desert and the rice plain. For two centuries it kept the road, until Băng Tâm Các and Phượng Minh Cung went to war over the caravan road. From 724 the garrison held out for two years against Phượng Minh's fire, drinking the desert lake down to salt. In 726 Phượng Minh's fire broke Cô Thành; the lone fortress fell and the lake turned to salt. Soon after, the Pivot imposed a truce on the Desert Road and the border stayed where it was; Băng Tâm kept the ruin and never rebuilt it. Much of the trade it once guarded later moved to the sea road through Hồi Lan Thành.
places.art_brief: A small painted miniature of broken verticals on a flat white salt pan: a square fortress whose walls are fire-glazed black and cracked, one corner tower standing at full height and the others slumped into rubble, the signature element. White salt crust climbing the wall bases, a dry caravan track passing at one side. No intact roofs. Warm golden-hour light from the top left, stark shadows on the salt. No text, no people larger than specks, nothing outside the footprint.
